North Dakota Science Content Standards

FD1347D0DFE60131EB6768A86D17958E.description: Identify ways scientists work together to solve problems (e.g., share results, teamwork, investigate)

FD12B250DFE60131EB6568A86D17958E.description: Students understand the history and nature of science.

FD127010DFE60131EB6468A86D17958E.description: Standard 8: History and Nature of Science

FD122DA0DFE60131EB6368A86D17958E.description: Describe some things (e.g., UV Rays, secondhand smoke, pollution) from our environment that are harmful to people

FD11E820DFE60131EB6268A86D17958E.description: Identify personal choices (e.g., personal hygiene, nutrition, fitness, safety) that contribute to individual wellness

FD113EE0DFE60131EB6068A86D17958E.description: Students understand relations between science and personal, social, and environmental issues.

FD109A90DFE60131EB5E68A86D17958E.description: Explain how models (e.g., plastic animal figures, skeletal models) can be used to understand science

FD104EF0DFE60131EB5D68A86D17958E.description: Identify tools (e.g., ruler, hand lens, thermometer, balance) that are used to observe, measure, and investigate things they could not otherwise see, measure and do

FD0FC430DFE60131EB5B68A86D17958E.description: Students understand relations between science and technology.

FD0F2D90DFE60131EB5968A86D17958E.description: Explain how the moon appears slightly different every day, but looks nearly the same every four weeks

FD0EE840DFE60131EB5868A86D17958E.description: Describe how the sun provides light and heat to warm the earth (e.g., land, air, and water)

FD0E6080DFE60131EB5668A86D17958E.description: Explain how fossils provide evidence about plants and animals and their environments that lived long ago (e.g., wooly mammoth, fern, ice age).

FD0E1DB0DFE60131EB5568A86D17958E.description: Identify different physical properties (e.g., size, shape, texture) of earth materials (e.g., rocks, sand, water)

FD0D8950DFE60131EB5368A86D17958E.description: Describe the patterns and characteristics of the four seasons, and how these changes in weather influence plant, animal, and human activities.

FD0CFAD0DFE60131EB5168A86D17958E.description: Students understand the basic concepts and principles of earth and space science.

FD0C57E0DFE60131EB4F68A86D17958E.description: Identify various things that are found in different environments (e.g., cactus, lizard – desert; shark, coral- ocean)

FD0BA160DFE60131EB4D68A86D17958E.description: Identify how plants and animals are alike and different (e.g., in the way they look, in their behaviors)

FD0B1DB0DFE60131EB4B68A86D17958E.description: Students understand the basic concepts and principles of life science.

FD0A9EA0DFE60131EB4968A86D17958E.description: Identify whether sources of heat and light are natural or human-made (e.g., sunlight, light bulb)

FD0A1B30DFE60131EB4768A86D17958E.description: Describe how objects fall unless something holds them up (e.g., apple on a tree, coat on a hook, pencil rolling off a desk)

FD09C970DFE60131EB4668A86D17958E.description: Describe an object's location (e.g., further than, beside, under, over) relative to another object

FD094290DFE60131EB4468A86D17958E.description: Sort matter by observable properties (e.g., size, shape, texture, color)

FD08FE80DFE60131EB4368A86D17958E.description: Explain why water left in an open container disappears, but water in a closed container does not disappear

FD08B9B0DFE60131EB4268A86D17958E.description: Identify ways (e.g., mixing, heating, cooling, cutting) to make changes in matter

FD081F10DFE60131EB4068A86D17958E.description: Students understand the basic concepts and principles of physical science.

FD0789B0DFE60131EB3E68A86D17958E.description: Communicate (e.g., verbal, written, graphic) observations to others

FD0743C0DFE60131EB3D68A86D17958E.description: Ask questions and seek answers about the world (e.g., Why do we have seasons?)

FD06F4E0DFE60131EB3C68A86D17958E.description: Abilities Necessary to do Scientific Inquiry

FD06A390DFE60131EB3B68A86D17958E.description: Students use the process of science inquiry.

FD15AE20DFE60131EB6F68A86D17958E.description: Identify some things that may not work if some of their parts are missing, broken, or assembled incorrectly (e.g., batteries are necessary for some toys to operate, wheels are necessary for a car to function)

FD1524A0DFE60131EB6D68A86D17958E.description: Identify changes that are slow (e.g., human development) or fast (e.g., plant growth)

FD148540DFE60131EB6B68A86D17958E.description: Explain ways models are like (e.g., globe and Earth are both round) and unlike (e.g., different sizes, missing details and functions) real things

FD13D6A0DFE60131EB6968A86D17958E.description: Students understand the unifying concepts and processes of science.

document.title: North Dakota Social Studies Content Standards

FF4B2600DFE60131EF6568A86D17958E.description: Describe how genetic, cognitive and physical development affect human behavior (e.g., inherited traits, development of self, deviant behavior and personality disorders)

FF4AA0F0DFE60131EF6368A86D17958E.description: Analyze conflict, cooperation, and interdependence among individuals, groups, and institutions (e.g., gender roles, social stratification, racial/ethnic bias)

FF4A5CB0DFE60131EF6268A86D17958E.description: Relate elements of socio-cultural development with other factors (e.g., individual differences, personality and assessment, psychological disorders and treatments)

FF4A1530DFE60131EF6168A86D17958E.description: Explain the various purposes of social groups, general implications of group membership, and different ways that groups function (e.g., minority groups, cliques, counterculture, family relations and political groups)

FF49BC50DFE60131EF6068A86D17958E.description: Explain how group and cultural influences contribute to human development, identity, and behavior (e.g., religion, education, media, government, and economy)

FF4930D0DFE60131EF5E68A86D17958E.description: Students understand the importance of culture, individual identity, and group identity.

FF48A150DFE60131EF5C68A86D17958E.description: Interpret the relationships between physical environments and society (e.g., humans modify environment, environment modifies society, and use, distribution, and importance of resources)

FF485090DFE60131EF5B68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the Earth's human systems (e.g., population, culture, settlement, economic interdependence)

FF479CF0DFE60131EF5968A86D17958E.description: Students understand and apply concepts of geography.

FF4717B0DFE60131EF5768A86D17958E.description: Evaluate the rights and responsibilities of citizenship and civic participation (e.g., election system and process; naturalization; political activism)

FF468950DFE60131EF5568A86D17958E.description: Analyze historical and contemporary examples of civil liberties and civil rights in the U.S. (e.g., incorporation of the Bill of Rights, amendments, key legislation, and landmark Supreme Court cases)

FF463E60DFE60131EF5468A86D17958E.description: Evaluate the effectiveness of structures, operations, and influences of political systems and constitutional governments (e.g., federalism; separation of powers; checks and balances; media and special interest groups)

FF45A420DFE60131EF5268A86D17958E.description: Analyze the content and context of documents, events, and organizations that influenced and established the United States (e.g., Magna Carta; English common law; Petition of Right; English Bill of Rights; 1st and 2nd Continental Congresses; Common Sense; Declaration of Independence, American Revolution Articles of Confederation; Constitutional Convention; Federalist Papers, Anti-Federalist Papers; U.S. Constitution, Bill of Rights)

FF455DE0DFE60131EF5168A86D17958E.description: Compare the nature and source of various types of political entities past and present throughout the world (e.g., ancient Greek and Roman political thought; classical republicans; philosophy of natural rights; limited and unlimited governments; constitutional governments; representative democracy; con-federal, federal, unitary systems of government, and international organizations)

FF44CD10DFE60131EF4F68A86D17958E.description: Explain how political and economic forces have affected the sovereignty of tribal nations (e.g., constitutional provisions; Supreme Court cases; laws used in forming the basis of the federal-tribal relationship; political and economic forces affecting sovereignty of tribal nations)

FF443690DFE60131EF4D68A86D17958E.description: Students understand the development, functions, and forms of various political institutions and the role of the citizen in government and society.

FF439F80DFE60131EF4B68A86D17958E.description: Interpret the concepts of exchange and trade and the impacts and implications of a global economy for individuals and nations

FF430510DFE60131EF4968A86D17958E.description: Analyze the role government plays in an economy (e.g., provision of public goods and services, taxes, protection of property rights, resolution of market failures)

FF42B340DFE60131EF4868A86D17958E.description: Describe the difference between the structure and operation of market economies and centrally planned or command economies (e.g., security, freedom, equity, efficiency, stability, growth)

FF426A70DFE60131EF4768A86D17958E.description: Explain the role of money and the role of financial institutions in a market economy (e.g., basic functions of money, composition of money supply, role of banks and other financial institutions, federal reserve, credit savings)

FF41D730DFE60131EF4568A86D17958E.description: Analyze basic micro and macro economic concepts (e.g., scarcity, opportunity cost, trade offs, markets, business organizations, factors of production, supply and demand, and personal finance)

FF414550DFE60131EF4368A86D17958E.description: Students understand economic concepts and the characteristics of various economic systems.

FF4080B0DFE60131EF4168A86D17958E.description: Explain contemporary issues and events in an interdependent world (e.g., trends in science, technology, and communication; religious conflicts; environmentalism; human rights and regional conflicts; apartheid, ethnic cleansing, role of United Nations and other international organizations such as UNICEF, GATT, NATO, OAS, World Bank, International Monetary Fund)

FF403070DFE60131EF4068A86D17958E.description: Analyze political and social change in the Middle East and Asia from 1948 – present (e.g., Camp David Accords, Tiananmen Square, conflicts in Middle East, Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, Persian Gulf War, War in Iraq)

FF3FEC60DFE60131EF3F68A86D17958E.description: Explain events in the development of the Cold War (e.g., Berlin Blockade; nuclear arms and space race; Cuban Missile Crisis; political and economic transformation of Western and Eastern Europe; Korean Conflict, Vietnam Conflict; collapse of Warsaw Pact Nations)

FF3FA7B0DFE60131EF3E68A86D17958E.description: Explain nationalist and revolutionary movements and attempts by colonial countries to achieve independence after World War II (e.g., revolutionary movements in China, Vietnam, Korea, Kenya, Pakistan, Indonesia, India, Northern Ireland, Chile)

FF3F6540DFE60131EF3D68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the global causes, course, and consequences of World War II and the post-war events (e.g., worldwide depression, totalitarian and militaristic regimes, Holocaust, political and social change in the Middle East, development of the United Nations, Cold War)

FF3F21B0DFE60131EF3C68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the global causes, course, and consequences of World War I (e.g. imperialism, militarism, nationalism, alliance system; ethnic conflicts and assassination of Arch Duke Franz Ferdinand; Russian Revolution of 1917; Treaty of Versailles and League of Nations)

FF3EDBF0DFE60131EF3B68A86D17958E.description: Compare the political, social, and industrial revolutions from the late 18th to the early 20th century (e.g., revolutions in the Americas and France; significant events and impacts of the Agricultural and the Industrial Revolution, Boer Wars, Boxer Rebellion, Sepoy rebellion)

FF3E8E40DFE60131EF3A68A86D17958E.description: Explain the growth and expansion of global economies and their impact on world regions (e.g., mercantilism, slavery, colonialism, Silk Road, salt trade)

FF3E3FA0DFE60131EF3968A86D17958E.description: Analyze the ideas, events and global impacts of the Renaissance, Reformation, Scientific Revolution, and the Enlightenment

FF3DED30DFE60131EF3868A86D17958E.description: Global Periods, Events, Figures, and Movements Including but not Limited to Renaissance to Present

FF3D95A0DFE60131EF3768A86D17958E.description: Analyze the major social issues and popular culture of contemporary US (e.g., immigration, environment, poverty, terrorism, and discrimination)

FF3D4B30DFE60131EF3668A86D17958E.description: Analyze the key events, and foreign and domestic policies of contemporary presidential administrations (e.g., Great Society, Watergate, relations with the Middle East; the Iranian hostage crisis; energy crisis; Reaganomics, Persian Gulf War)

FF3CEC20DFE60131EF3568A86D17958E.description: Analyze the key events and political/social effects of the Vietnam conflict (e.g., Gulf of Tonkin Resolution and the Tet Offensive; protests and opposition; presidential policies, War Powers Act)

FF3CA550DFE60131EF3468A86D17958E.description: Analyze the struggle for equal opportunity (e.g., Civil Rights Movement, Martin Luther King, Jr., Malcolm X, civil rights legislation and court cases, civil rights organizations, National Organization for Women, Equal Rights Amendment, American Indian Movement, Caesar Chavez)

FF3C5F90DFE60131EF3368A86D17958E.description: Analyze the origins, foreign policy, events, and domestic consequences of the Cold War (e.g., containment policy, arms race, fear of communism)

FF3C15F0DFE60131EF3268A86D17958E.description: Analyze the economic boom and social transformation of post WWII America (e.g., popular culture, changing women's roles, technological developments)

FF3BBD10DFE60131EF3168A86D17958E.description: Trace the causes, course, and legacy of World War II (e.g., totalitarian regimes; Pacific theater, European theater, home front)

FF3B61D0DFE60131EF3068A86D17958E.description: Analyze the major political, economic, and social developments that occurred between World War I and World War II (e.g. Red Scare, Roaring 20's, Great Depression, New Deal)

FF3B1040DFE60131EF2F68A86D17958E.description: Trace the causes, course, and legacy of the United States' involvement in World War I at home and abroad (e.g., neutrality, military technologies, isolationism, Zimmerman Note, Lusitania, home front, Wilson's Fourteen Points)

FF3ACAE0DFE60131EF2E68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate the impact of various factors that led to the transformation of the nation (e.g., imperialism, industrialization, immigration, political/social reformers, urbanization, mechanization of agriculture, changing business environment)

FF3A8AF0DFE60131EF2D68A86D17958E.description: U.S. Periods, Events, Figures, Movements to Include but not Limited to Industrialization to Present

FF3A4810DFE60131EF2C68A86D17958E.description: Analyze Federal policy and action regarding American Indians (e.g. Dawes Act, changes in federal and state Indian policies, civil rights movement; current issues surrounding gaming, housing, distribution of wealth, and healthcare, Indian Reorganization Act, Bureau of Indian Affairs, Indian Civil Rights Act, Indian Child Welfare Act, American Indian Religious Freedom Act, Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, Citizenship, American Indian Movement)

FF392F40DFE60131EF2868A86D17958E.description: Analyze the impact of bias and prejudice in historical and contemporary media

FF38AEA0DFE60131EF2668A86D17958E.description: Apply social studies skills (e.g., recognize cause and effect, trends, multiple perspectives, change) in real-life contexts (e.g., backtracking current global issues, Model U.N., mock trials, simulated congressional hearings, parliamentary debates, comparative statistical analysis, mental maps, GPS, GIS).

FF386D80DFE60131EF2568A86D17958E.description: Use media (e.g., oral, written, websites, computer simulations, multimedia resources) to access, record, analyze, and communicate information relating to social studies

FF382990DFE60131EF2468A86D17958E.description: Draw conclusions based on the research processes (e.g., collect, organize, evaluate, and synthesize information)

FF378D40DFE60131EF2268A86D17958E.description: Interpret and evaluate a variety of visual representations (e.g. charts, graphs, time lines, graphic organizers, maps, flow charts) of data

FF36FDA0DFE60131EF2068A86D17958E.description: Interpret and evaluate documents (e.g., primary and secondary sources, fact, fiction, or opinion) to enhance the understanding of social studies content.

FF3672A0DFE60131EF1E68A86D17958E.description: Students apply Social Studies skills and resources.

document.title: North Dakota Social Studies Content Standards

FEDABD00DFE60131EE8868A86D17958E.description: Explain the cultural differences (e.g., traditions, celebrations, food) in the regions of the United States today

FEDA6F20DFE60131EE8768A86D17958E.description: Identify examples of conflict (e.g., slavery, war, gender roles) and cooperation (e.g., settlements) that occurred among cultures (e.g., gender, ethnic groups, religious groups, immigrant groups, socio-economic status)

FED9E9C0DFE60131EE8568A86D17958E.description: Students understand the importance of culture, individual identity, and group identity.

FED96080DFE60131EE8368A86D17958E.description: Explain how human activity (e.g., settlement patterns, migration) affects the physical environment (e.g., soil uses, economy, pollution, use of energy sources)

FED91950DFE60131EE8268A86D17958E.description: Explain the impact of geography on western exploration and westward migration in the early nineteenth century (e.g., Northwest passage, colonization, Appalachian Mountains)

FED8CCD0DFE60131EE8168A86D17958E.description: Explain the impact of climate, geography, and available resources on the daily lives of Native Americans (e.g., dwellings, clothes, food and crops, technology, tools, cultural traditions)

FED83EC0DFE60131EE7F68A86D17958E.description: Students understand and apply concepts of geography.

FED7A860DFE60131EE7D68A86D17958E.description: Explain why the United States government is necessary (e.g., government helps secure people's lives, liberty, and property through law and military protection; groups can accomplish things collectively that individuals cannot)

FED758C0DFE60131EE7C68A86D17958E.description: Identify the purpose and importance behind documents leading up to the writing of the United States Constitution and the Bill of Rights (e.g., Magna Carta, English common law, English Bill of Rights, Declaration of Independence, Articles of Confederation)

FED71330DFE60131EE7B68A86D17958E.description: Identify the duties of the executive, judicial, and legislative branches of the Federal government (e.g., checks and balances)

FED681E0DFE60131EE7968A86D17958E.description: Identify the roles, rights, and responsibilities of U.S. citizens in a democratic society (e.g., the responsibility to pay taxes, the responsibility to sit on a jury)

FED5CC80DFE60131EE7768A86D17958E.description: Students understand the development, functions, and forms of various political institutions and the role of the citizen in government and society.

FED53AB0DFE60131EE7568A86D17958E.description: Describe the basic concepts of imports, exports, and international trade

FED4F610DFE60131EE7468A86D17958E.description: Describe the concept of competition and its relationship to price (e.g., market based economy)

FED4B1A0DFE60131EE7368A86D17958E.description: Explain the relationships between scarcity and resources (e.g., home building materials, food, clothing, hunting)

FED426E0DFE60131EE7168A86D17958E.description: Describe how various non-economic factors (e.g., culture, values, interests) can influence economic behaviors and decision making

FED38B80DFE60131EE6F68A86D17958E.description: Students understand economic concepts and the characteristics of various economic systems.

FED2F4E0DFE60131EE6D68A86D17958E.description: Explain reasons for early exploration (e.g., search for Northwest passage, "gold, glory, and God," riches, trade)

FED2A230DFE60131EE6C68A86D17958E.description: Explain how regional Native American groups influenced U.S. history (e.g., historical events, development of the U. S.)

FED24A10DFE60131EE6B68A86D17958E.description: Describe the migration patterns of people from Asia to the Americas during the Ice Age (e.g., regional patterns, migration and settlement of the first Americans in the Western Hemisphere)

FED1B960DFE60131EE6968A86D17958E.description: Analyze the events and consequences of the Revolutionary War (e.g., Lexington, Concord, Bunker Hill, Benedict Arnold, Valley Forge)

FED174D0DFE60131EE6868A86D17958E.description: Identify the reasons (e.g., Boston Tea Party, the Stamp Act, English Laws) for conflict between England and the American colonies and the key people (e.g., George Washington, King George III, John Adams, Paul Revere) involved

FED13050DFE60131EE6768A86D17958E.description: Describe the daily lives of people from different social groups (e.g., large landowners, farmers, artisans, women, slaves) in colonial America

FED0EAE0DFE60131EE6668A86D17958E.description: Explain how conflicts and cooperation between the Native Americans and Europeans (e.g., French and Indian Wars, trade) influenced colonial events

FED0A260DFE60131EE6568A86D17958E.description: Explain reasons for early colonization (e.g., religious freedom, economic opportunity)

FECFFBE0DFE60131EE6368A86D17958E.description: Describe similarities and differences between past events and current events in U.S. history (e.g., in the lives of people from different cultures past and present)

FECFBD20DFE60131EE6268A86D17958E.description: Use chronological order and sequence to describe cause-and-effect relationships of U.S. historical events (e.g., how Columbian Exchange impacted local people)

FECF4030DFE60131EE6068A86D17958E.description: Explain the significance of scientists, inventors, and historical figures (e.g., Christopher Columbus, Juan Ponce De Leon, Benjamin Franklin, George Washington, Paul Revere, Benjamin Rush, David Rittenhouse, Thomas Paine)

FECEB460DFE60131EE5E68A86D17958E.description: Explain the significance of America's symbols (e.g., Pledge of Allegiance, Statue of Liberty, Liberty Bell, American flag, Star Spangled Banner)

FECD9E00DFE60131EE5A68A86D17958E.description: Use spatial terms to describe the world (i.e., Tropic of Cancer, Tropic of Capricorn, International Dateline, Arctic Circle, Antarctic Circle)

FECD1F20DFE60131EE5868A86D17958E.description: Construct and interpret time lines of key events in United States history

FECC8170DFE60131EE5668A86D17958E.description: Evaluate current events using print and electronic media (e.g., newspaper, children's news magazines, television, Internet)

FECC39A0DFE60131EE5568A86D17958E.description: Identify differences between primary and secondary resources (e.g., maps, charts, line and bar graphs, Internet, atlases, journals, letters, photographs, interviews, periodicals)

FECBB4B0DFE60131EE5368A86D17958E.description: Interpret and compare maps of the United States (i.e., political, physical, thematic)

FECB2800DFE60131EE5168A86D17958E.description: Students apply Social Studies skills and resources.

document.title: North Dakota English Language Arts and Literacy Content Standards

5FB0A053C15F42609C12EA9D1CB2BE58.description: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases; gather vocabulary knowledge when considering a word or phrase important to comprehension or expression.

7E65FAD5E1CB4E869EB011EC11FAEBAB.description: Compare two decimals to hundredths by reasoning about their size. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two decimals refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual model.

BBED2F35286840399CD0795BA8941CD1.description: Use decimal notation for fractions with denominators 10 or 100.
comments: For example, rewrite 0.62 as 62/100; describe a length as 0.62 meters; locate 0.62 on a number line diagram.

B0758394DDA6411997D82E3BC748F81F.description: Express a fraction with denominator 10 as an equivalent fraction with denominator 100, and use this technique to add two fractions with respective denominators 10 and 100.
comments: Students who can generate equivalent fractions can develop strategies for adding fractions with unlike denominators in general. But addition and subtraction with unlike denominators in general is not a requirement at this grade.
For example, express 3/10 as 30/100, and add 3/10 + 4/100 = 34/100.

6B230EC851BC4D739618D532FE360A72.description: Understand decimal notation for fractions, and compare decimal fractions.

comments: For example, if each person at a party will eat 3/8 of a pound of roast beef, and there will be 5 people at the party, how many pounds of roast beef will be needed? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?
A87F8E4AD4CD47D296B886623062EA47.description: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.

F5EF8D11A9CE4837A475B5406419D2A4.description: Understand a multiple of a/b as a multiple of 1/b, and use this understanding to multiply a fraction by a whole number.
comments: For example, use a visual fraction model to express 3 × (2/5) as 6 × (1/5), recognizing this product as 6/5. (In general, n × (a/b) = (n × a)/b.)
For example, use a visual fraction model to represent 5/4 as the product 5 × (1/4), recording the conclusion by the equation 5/4 = 5 × (1/4).
DB87192DD71548B1AE0B74EC47AFDA5E.description: Understand a fraction a/b as a multiple of 1/b.

AB40D6D68B7549C38B8C05024591E557.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction by a whole number.

8DB5AA71A8E446D4A1A3A1CF255FCF3E.description: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and having like denominators, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.

864C5AFF4B6E4A7EB38DB9CBCC2580CC.description: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators, e.g., by replacing each mixed number with an equivalent fraction, and/or by using properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction.

C4F1046A66F34D2289FE81854EDED0C8.description: Decompose a fraction into a sum of fractions with the same denominator in more than one way, recording each decomposition by an equation. Justify decompositions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

68BC152863E54BB1AC820F51486AC59C.description: Understand addition and subtraction of fractions as joining and separating parts referring to the same whole.

9136E3DEA47F4E7E9061393461BA2368.description: Understand a fraction a/b with a > 1 as a sum of fractions 1/b.

8E477654EDFC4BF3B180C42AA4F3F730.description: Build fractions from unit fractions by applying and extending previous understandings of operations on whole numbers.

D0CFC48F7B884A6DA6EA5E02170D55A0.description: Compare two fractions with different numerators and different denominators, e.g., by creating common denominators or numerators, or by comparing to a benchmark fraction such as 1/2. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

AD429B96E47E4FD9860B9FDBFCB54FEE.description: Explain why a fraction a/b is equivalent to a fraction (n × a)/(n × b) by using visual fraction models, with attention to how the number and size of the parts differ even though the two fractions themselves are the same size. Use this principle to recognize and generate equivalent fractions.

A293294625604FBC90C8DF5092CF0724.description: Extend understanding of fraction equivalence and ordering.

comments: Grade 3 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8.
Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 100

14EED5E018B44CA6B22C50FEFCA0AB24.description: Recognize a line of symmetry for a two-dimensional figure as a line across the figure such that the figure can be folded along the line into matching parts. Identify line-symmetric figures and draw lines of symmetry.

2056C27DF174464D9EE385E886B06AC1.description: Classify two-dimensional figures based on the presence or absence of parallel or perpendicular lines, or the presence or absence of angles of a specified size. Recognize right triangles as a category, and identify right triangles.

9A0F5B9A8A574E55BCF18B720512BB61.description: Draw points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (right, acute, obtuse), and perpendicular and parallel lines. Identify these in two-dimensional figures.

96701D4CCEFE45668909E7D55AD76E3D.description: Draw and identify lines and angles, and classify shapes by properties of their lines and angles.

9D1A59526EC24E378125016F50AEBCA1.description: Recognize angle measure as additive. Solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram in real world and mathematical problems, e.g., by using an equation with a symbol for the unknown angle measure.

A7E51E6545744306B811C2BBC602521F.description: Measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor. Sketch angles of specified measure.

1F36ECF203BF4470B2A1357B14C90241.description: An angle that turns through n one-degree angles is said to have an angle measure of n degrees.

29E8CEFF30364D27B755176BD8A04ECF.description: An angle is measured with reference to a circle with its center at the common endpoint of the rays, by considering the fraction of the circular arc between the points where the two rays intersect the circle. An angle that turns through 1/360 of a circle is called a "one-degree angle," and can be used to measure angles.

C5EE2FFE8C49446595047719CE3ACF19.description: Recognize angles as geometric shapes that are formed wherever two rays share a common endpoint, and understand concepts of angle measurement:

comments: For example, from a line plot find and interpret the difference in length between the longest and shortest specimens in an insect collection.
4E106042895845AD9A83A038A16B5552.description: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions by using information presented in line plots.

9EF07B5C54D04C7EA94A3ACF77670FFD.description: Apply the area and perimeter formulas for rectangles in real world and mathematical problems.
comments: For example, find the width of a rectangular room given the area of the flooring and the length, by viewing the area formula as a multiplication equation with an unknown factor.

D097EA3A7B32418A8182E7698EEF362D.description: Use the four operations to solve word problems involving distances, intervals of time, liquid volumes, masses of objects, and money, including problems involving simple fractions or decimals, and problems that require expressing measurements given in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit. Represent measurement quantities using diagrams such as number line diagrams that feature a measurement scale.

comments: For example, know that 1 ft is 12 times as long as 1 in. Express the length of a 4 ft snake as 48 in. Generate a conversion table for feet and inches listing the number pairs (1, 12), (2, 24), (3, 36), …
B4C808D965964EFEA787AE0F3CBB0CC0.description: Know relative sizes of measurement units within one system of units including km, m, cm; kg, g; lb, oz.; l, ml; hr, min, sec. Within a single system of measurement, express measurements in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit. Record measurement equivalents in a two column table.

B89AE2A110C74474BC34090E6080DF35.description: Solve problems involving measurement and conversion of measurements from a larger unit to a smaller unit.

1B4F4CE29134497EBDD6AEA04EC216C7.description: Find whole-number quotients and remainders with up to four-digit dividends and one-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

8ECC2C42E9D4484B857FF42ED718ECA1.description: Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit whole number, and multiply two two-digit numbers, using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

56664E45B7AE462DA55E5397571C5408.description: Fluently add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.

1E45187B403140EA937B63D2B7FD1B29.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic.

0692605428744F3083993DAD0B83C50F.description: Use place value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place.

BFA38E80DFB04E6884CBED5D08099BA4.description: Read and write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form. Compare two multi-digit numbers based on meanings of the digits in each place, using >, =, and < symbols to record the results of comparisons.

comments: For example, recognize that 700 ÷ 70 = 10 by applying concepts of place value and division.
9F31333807F9499FBEE430CFA16F20AA.description: Recognize that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right.

1C4E8F67759E4CFDA86CD26A26D75A08.description: Generalize place value understanding for multi-digit whole numbers.

69D07EF5676542F2917BD5AB57B1CDE7.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

FF84F3D713E24BAEB157EFA977999E99.description: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself.
comments: For example, given the rule "Add 3" and the starting number 1, generate terms in the resulting sequence and observe that the terms appear to alternate between odd and even numbers. Explain informally why the numbers will continue to alternate in this way.

D7DB11CCCB56435CB96634FF4DF3CDF7.description: Find all factor pairs for a whole number in the range 1—100. Recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1—100 is a multiple of a given one-digit number. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1—100 is prime or composite.

410C843221AF452086A5DBD8D3E5774D.description: Gain familiarity with factors and multiples.

94CA5ED6D60D4CD3B8E85414FBB7B574.description: Solve multistep word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.

FB976D61DA6B43A89856CC4E146369FB.description: Multiply or divide to solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem, distinguishing multiplicative comparison from additive comparison.

125EC6F16E5949BDA5E707A642AB8523.description: Interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison, e.g., interpret 35 = 5 × 7 as a statement that 35 is 5 times as many as 7 and 7 times as many as 5. Represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as multiplication equations.

2E02B7BD98A14BB48E437FF01FDC9F70.description: Use the four operations with whole numbers to solve problems.

70B5E22D334D4D6DA9A3F47363D08A44.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

3DB45C9748784831AA0B3BFB3C5FA0F0.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

2AB8214BF103493CBE613239A2E73B5C.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

F7E7001BF4904367AA1D263E3AE55962.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

Example: Knowing that 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16, one can find 8 × 7 as 8 × (5 + 2) = (8 × 5) + (8 × 2) = 40 + 16 = 56. (Distributive property.)

Example: If 6 × 4 = 24 is known, then 4 × 6 = 24 is also known (Commutative property of multiplication.) 3 × 5 × 2 can be found by 3 × 5 = 15, then 15 × 2 = 30, or by 5 × 2 = 10, then 3 × 10 = 30. (Associative property of multiplication.)

561E0317FEA346BF807292C005B74DFD.description: Represent and solve problems involving multiplication and division.

comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
311912E0ED414617A035FFD66E70F709.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.
6AEC990400E04157963178F1CF2739DA.description: Look for and make use of structure.

comments: Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
53B9D649C4C74B18B9582110D7E91AF1.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.
1DD13051CF8242EE828807E215286ABA.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

4365D6A58E2D4D69B789250E932B62E2.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

AD8550A7CB3A435FB6D5E7445414C875.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
B0C27046B89E45E19383A61A2A176F1F.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.
82B9DEF0D011475F88A307A5D61DC2A2.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

961854C0516C495A8D61D57140CCEF61.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

D39C38DD0A634372839AAA630A1C6C2B.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
F3B95C927C1142ABB28FAD04CC904567.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.
7F3AC537E6564A35A1C45C6F94385E3B.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

document.title: North Dakota Social Studies Content Standards

FF2B44A0DFE60131EF1B68A86D17958E.description: Explain how culture influences gender roles, ethics, and beliefs

FF272040DFE60131EF0D68A86D17958E.description: Explain the political party process at the local, state, and national level (e.g., the structure and functions of political parties, electoral college, how campaigns are run and who participates in them, the role of the media in the election process, various kinds of elections)

FF22A700DFE60131EEFE68A86D17958E.description: Explain the significance of key events (e.g., settlement and homesteading, statehood, reservations) and people (e.g., Roughrider Recipients) in North Dakota and tribal history

FF222980DFE60131EEFC68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the impact of immigration on the United States (e.g., labor pools, ghettos)

FF21E960DFE60131EEFB68A86D17958E.description: Trace the social, economic, political, and cultural factors of Reconstruction (e.g., Jim Crow Laws, election of 1876, black codes, rise of Ku Klux Klan)

FF20DD80DFE60131EEF768A86D17958E.description: Explain how the concept of Manifest Destiny impacted national policy (e.g., War with Mexico, Gadsden Purchase, imperialism, Gold Rush, foreign policy)

FF209D80DFE60131EEF668A86D17958E.description: Explain how political leaders (e.g., Andrew Jackson, William Henry Harrison, Martin Van Buren, John Tyler) dictated national policy (e.g., States' rights, closure of National Bank, Indian Removal Act)

FF205B20DFE60131EEF568A86D17958E.description: Explain how political parties developed to resolve issues (e.g., payment of debt, establishment of a national bank, strict or loose interpretation of the Constitution, support for England or France) in the early years of the United States

FF2018F0DFE60131EEF468A86D17958E.description: Analyze the transformation of the nation (e.g., Imperialism, industrialization, immigration, political/social reformers, urbanization, mechanization of agriculture, changing business environment)
